# [Friday 13 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/13/)

Up, lying long all alone ([my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) lying for these two or three days of sickness alone), thinking of my several businesses in hand, and then rose and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), being in some doubt of having my cozen [Roger](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/247/) and [Lord Hinchinbroke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/113/) and [Sir Thos. Crew](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/773/) by my cozens invitation at dinner to-day, and we wholly unprovided. So I away to Westminster, to the Parliament-door, to speak with Roger: and here I saw my [Lord Keeling](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11343/) go into [the House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/292/) to the barr, to have his business heard by the whole House to-day; and a great crowd of people to stare upon him. Here I hear that the Lords’ Bill for banishing and disabling my [Lord Clarendon](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/) from bearing any office, or being in [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) dominions, and its being made felony for any to correspond with him but his own children, is brought to the [Commons](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/292/): but they will not agree to it, being not satisfied with that as sufficient, but will have a Bill of Attainder brought in against him: but they make use of this against the [Lords](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/293/), that they, that would not think there was cause enough to commit him without hearing, will have him banished without hearing. By and by comes out my cozen Roger to me, he being not willing to be in the House at the business of my Lord Keeling, lest he should be called upon to complain against him for his abusing him at [Cambridge](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2589/), very wrongfully and shamefully, but not to his reproach, but to the Chief justice’s in the end, when all the world cried shame upon him for it. So he with me [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/), whom I took up by the way, going thither, and they to dine with me, and pretty merry, and among other pieces of news, it is now fresh that the [King of Portugall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5040/) is deposed, and [his brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11924/) made King; and that my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) is gone from [Madrid](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11925/) with great honour to [Lisbon](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10946/), to make up, at this juncture, a peace to the advantage, as [the Spaniard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10146/) would have it, of Spain. I wish it may be for my Lord’s honour, if it be so; but it seems my Lord is in mighty estimation in Spain. After dinner comes [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/), and he and I alone a while, he telling me my Lord Sandwich’s credit is like to be undone, if the bill of 200 _l._ my Lord Hinchingbroke wrote to me about be not paid to-morrow, and that, if I do not help him about it, they have no way but to let it be protested. So, finding that Creed hath supplied them with 150 _l._ in their straits, and that this is no bigger sum, I am very willing to serve my Lord, though not in this kind; but yet I will endeavour to get this done for them, and the rather because of some [plate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7982/) that was lodged the other day with me, by [my Lady’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/115/) order, which may be in part of security for my money, as I may order it, for, for ought I see, there is no other to be hoped for. This do trouble me; but yet it is good luck that the sum is no bigger. He gone, I with my cozen Roger to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/); and there we met the House rising: and they have voted my Lord Chief Justice Keeling’s proceedings illegal; but that, out of particular respect to him, and the mediation of a great many, they have resolved to proceed no further against him. After a turn or two with my cozen, I away with [Sir W. Warren](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1748/), who met me here by my desire, and to [Exeter House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/103/), and there to counsel, to [Sir William Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10991/), about the business of my bargain with my [Lady Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1572/); and he do give me good advice, and that I am safe, but that there is a great many pretty considerations in it that makes it necessary for me to be silent yet for a while till we see whether [the ship](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10396/) be safe or no; for she is drove to the coast of Holland, where she now is in the [Texell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8500/), so that it is not prudence for me yet to resolve whether I will stand by the bargain or no, and so home, and Sir W. Warren and I walked upon [Tower Hill](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1395/) by moonlight a great while, consulting business of the office and our present condition, which is but bad, it being most likely that the Parliament will change all hands, and so let them, so I may keep but what I have. Thence home, and there spent the evening at home with my wife and entering my journal, and so to supper and to bed, troubled with my parting with the 200 _l._, which I must lend my Lord Sandwich to answer his [bill of exchange](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14187/).

# [Saturday 14 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/14/)

Up and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where busy, and after dinner also to the office again till night, when [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/) come to me to discourse about the 200 _l._ I must supply my [Lord Hinchingbroke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/113/), and I promised him to do it, though much against my will. So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), to supper and to bed.

# [Sunday 15 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/15/)

(Lord’s day). Up, and [to church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), where I heard [a German](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11926/) preach, in a tone hard to be understood, but yet an extraordinary good sermon, and wholly to my great content. So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there all alone with [wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and [girle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) to dinner, and then I busy at my chamber all the afternoon, and looking over my [plate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7982/), which indeed is a very fine quantity, God knows, more than ever I expected to see of my own, and more than is fit for a man of no better quality than I am. In the evening comes [Mrs. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3028/) to visit us, who hath been long sick, and she sat and supped with us, and after supper, her son [Francke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11013/) being there, now upon the point of his going to the [East Indys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/636/), I did give him [“Lex Mercatoria,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11927/) and my wife my old pair of tweezers, which are pretty, and my book an excellent one for him. Most of our talk was of the great discourse the world hath against my [Lady Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1572/), for getting [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/) to give her all, and disinherit his [eldest son](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2215/); though the truth is, the son, as they say, did play the knave with his father when time was, and the father no great matter better with him, nor with other people also. So she gone, we to bed.

# [Monday 16 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/16/)

Up, and to several places, to pay what I owed. Among others, to my mercer, to pay for my fine [camlott](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11928/) cloak, which costs me, the very stuff, almost 6 _l._; and also a velvet coat — the outside cost me above 8 _l._. And so to Westminster, where I find [the House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/292/) mighty busy upon a petition against my [Lord Gerard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5794/), which lays heavy things to his charge, of his abusing [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) in his Guards; and very hot the House is upon it. I away [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner alone with [wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and [girle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/), and so to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where mighty busy to my great content late, and then home to supper, talk with my wife, and to bed. It was doubtful to-day whether the House should be adjourned to-morrow or no.

# [Tuesday 17 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/17/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where very busy all the morning, and then in the afternoon I with [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) and [Sir T. Harvy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8284/) to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/) to attend the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/), who is now as well as ever, and there we did our usual business with him, and so away home with Sir W. Pen, and there to the office, where pretty late doing business, [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) having been abroad all day with [Mrs. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3028/) buying of one thing or other. This day I do hear at White Hall that the [Duke of Monmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5315/) is sick, and in danger of the [smallpox](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/363/). So [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to supper and to bed.

# [Wednesday 18 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/18/)

Up, and to [my goldsmith’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9584/) in the morning, to look after the providing of 60 _l._ for [Mr. Moore](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/340/), towards the answering of my [Lord Sandwich’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/)[bill of exchange](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14187/), he being come to be contented with my lending him 60 _l._ in part of it, which pleases me, I expecting to have been forced to answer the whole bill; and this, which I do do, I hope to secure out of the [plate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7982/), which was delivered into my custody of my Lord’s the other day by [Mr. Cooke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/662/), and which I did get Mr. Stokes, the goldsmith, last night to weigh at my house, and there is enough to secure 100 _l._. Thence home to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there all the morning by particular appointment with [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/), [Sir R. Ford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1347/), and those that are concerned for my [Lady Batten](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1572/) ([Mr. Wood](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/615/), [Young](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2515/), and [Lewes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5018/)), to even the accounts of our [prize](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9633/) business, and at noon broke up, and to dinner, every man to his own home, and to it till late at night again, and we did come to some end, and I am mightily put to it how to order the business of my bargaine, but my industry is to keep it off from discourse till [the ship](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10396/) be brought home safe, and this I did do, and so we broke up, she appearing in our debts about 1500 _l._, and so we parted, and I to my business, and home to [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), who is troubled with the tooth ake, and there however I got her to read to me the [History of Algiers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11929/), which I find a very pretty book, and so to supper with much pleasure talking, and to bed. The [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) not adjourned yet.

# [Thursday 19 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/19/)

Up, and to [the Office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where [Commissioner Middleton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7120/) first took place at the [Board](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/482/) as [Surveyor of the Navy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/486/); and indeed I think will be an excellent officer; I am sure much beyond what his predecessor was. At noon, to avoid being forced to invite him to dinner, it being his first day, and nobody inviting him, I did go to [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/) with [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) in his coach, who first went to [Guildhall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/129/), whither I went with him, he to speak with [Sheriff Gawden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/) — I only for company; and did here look up and down this place, where I have not been before since [the fire](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10319/); and I see that [the city](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/) are got a pace on in the rebuilding of Guildhall. Thence to the ’Change, where I stayed very little, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and there find [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) mightily out of order with her teeth. At the office all the afternoon, and at night by coach to Westminster, to [the Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), where I met nobody, and do find that this evening [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) by message (which he never did before) hath passed several bills, among others that for the Accounts, and for banishing my [Lord Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/), and hath adjourned the House to February; at which I am glad, hoping in this time to get leisure to state my [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) Accounts, and to prepare better for the [Parliament’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) enquiries. Here I hear how the [House of Lords](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/293/), with great severity, if not tyranny, have ordered poor [Carr](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11437/), who only erred in the manner of the presenting his petition against my [Lord Gerard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5794/), it being first printed before it was presented; which was, it, seems, by [Colonel Sands’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11930/) going into the country, into whose hands he had put it: the poor man is ordered to stand in the pillory two or three times, and his eares cut, and be imprisoned I know not how long. But it is believed that the [Commons](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/292/), when they meet, will not be well pleased with it; and they have no reason, I think. Having only heard this from [Mrs. Michell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1101/), I away again home, and there to supper and to bed, my wife exceeding ill in her face with the tooth ake, and now her face has become mightily swelled that I am mightily troubled for it.

# [Friday 20 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/20/)

Up, and all the morning at [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) with [Sir R. Ford](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1347/) and the same company as on Wednesday about my [Lady Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1572/) accounts. At noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, where my poor [wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) in bed in mighty pain, her left cheek so swelled as that we feared it would break, and so were fain to send for [Mr. Hollier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1536/), who come, and seems doubtful of the defluxions of humours that may spoil her face, if not timely cured. He laid a poultice to it and other directions, and so away, and I to the office, where on the same accounts very late, and did come pretty near a settlement. So at night to [Sir W. Pen’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) with Sir R. Ford, and there was [Sir D. Gawden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/994/), and there we only talked of sundry things; and I have found of late, by discourse, that the present sort of government is looked upon as a sort of government that we never had yet — that is to say, a [King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) and [House of Commons](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/292/) against the [House of Lords](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/293/); for so indeed it is, though neither of the two first care a fig for one another, nor the third for them both, only the Bishops are afeard of losing ground, as I believe they will. So home to my poor wife, who is in mighty pain, and her face miserably swelled: so as I was frighted to see it, and I was forced to lie below in the great chamber, where I have not lain many a day, and having sat up with her, talking and reading and pitying her, I to bed.

# [Saturday 21 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/21/)

At [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) all the morning, and at noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner with my Clerks and [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/), who among other things all alone, after dinner, talking of the times, he tells me that the [Nonconformists](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/666/) are mighty high, and their meetings frequented and connived at; and they do expect to have their day now soon; for my [Lord of Buckingham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2558/) is a declared friend to them, and even to the [Quakers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/305/), who had very good words the other day from [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) himself: and, what is more, the [Archbishop of Canterbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2519/) is called no more to [the Cabal](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13278/), nor, by the way, [Sir W. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/); which I am sorry for, the Cabal at present being, as he says, the King, and Duke of Buckingham, and [Lord Keeper](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1427/), the [Duke of Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/), and [Privy Seale](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1219/). The Bishops, differing from the King in the late business in the [House of Lords](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/293/), having caused this and what is like to follow, for every body is encouraged nowadays to speak, and even to preach, as I have heard one of them, as bad things against them as ever in the year 1640; which is a strange change. He gone, I to the office, where busy till late at night, and then home to sit with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), who is a little better, and her cheek asswaged. I read to her out of [“The History of Algiers,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11929/) which is mighty pretty reading, and did discourse alone about my sister [Pall’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1568/) match, which is now on foot with one [Jackson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11931/), another nephew of [Mr. Phillips’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2785/), to whom he hath left his estate.

# [Sunday 22 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/22/)

(Lord’s day). Up, and [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), poor wretch, still in pain, and then to dress myself and down to my chamber to settle some papers, and thither come to me [Willet](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) with an errand from her mistress, and this time I first did give her a little kiss, she being a very pretty humoured girle, and so one that I do love mightily. Thence to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there did a little business, and so to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), where a dull sermon, and then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and [Cozen Kate Joyce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1105/) come and dined with me and [Mr. Holliard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1536/); but by chance I offering occasion to him to discourse of the [Church of Rome](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/306/), Lord! how he run on to discourse with the greatest vehemence and importunity in the world, as the only thing in the world that he is full of, and it was good sport to me to see him so earnest on so little occasion. She come to see us and to tell me that [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1107/) is going to build his house again, and would borrow of me 300 _l._, which I shall upon good security be willing to do, and so told her, being willing to have some money out of my hands upon good security. After dinner up to my wife again, who is in great pain still with her tooth, and there, they gone, I spent the most of the afternoon and night reading and talking to bear her company, and so to supper and to bed.

# [Monday 23 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/23/)

Up before day, and by coach to [Sir W. Coventry’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/), and with him to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there walked a great while with him in the garden till the [Commissioners of the Treasury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11226/) met, and there talked over many businesses, and particularly he tells me that by my desire he hath moved the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) that [Sir J. Minnes](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2463/) might be removed from the Navy, at least the [Controller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/485/) place, and his business put on my [Lord Brouncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) and [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/); that the [Committee for Accounts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/12029/) are good sober men, and such as he thinks we shall have fair play from; that he hopes that the kingdom will escape ruin in general, notwithstanding all our fears, and yet I find he do seem not very confident in it. So to the Commissioners of the Treasury, and there I had a dispute before them with [Sir Stephen Fox](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/848/) about our orders for money, who is very angry, but I value it not. But, Lord! to see with what folly my [Lord Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/) do speak in this business would make a man wonder at the good fortune of such a fool. Thence meeting there with [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/), he and I to [the Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1085/), and there I saw [Carr](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11437/) stand in the pillory for the business of my [Lord Gerard](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5794/), which is supposed will make a hot business in the [House of Commons](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/292/), when they shall come to sit again, the [Lords](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/293/) having ordered this with great injustice, as all people think, his only fault being the printing his petition before, by accident, his petition be read in the House. Here walked up and down the Exchange with Creed, and then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and there hear by Creed that the Bishops [of Winchester](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5744/) and [of Rochester, and the Dean of the Chapel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10263/), and some other great prelates, are suspended: and a cloud upon [the Archbishop](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2519/) ever since the late business in the House of Lords; and I believe it will be a heavy blow to the Clergy. This noon I bought [a sermon](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11955/) of [Dr. Floyd’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10568/), which Creed read a great part of to me and [Mr. Hollier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1536/), who dined with me, but as well writ and as good, against the Church of Rome, as ever I read; but, Lord! how Hollier, poor man, was taken with it. They gone I to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and there very late with [Mr. Willson](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6487/) and my people about the making of a new contract for the [victualler](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9082/), which do and will require a great deal of pains of me, and so to supper and to bed, [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) being pretty well all this day by reason of her imposthume being broke in her cheek into her mouth. This day, at the ’Change, Creed shewed me [Mr. Coleman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11315/), of whom my wife hath so good an opinion, and says that he is as very a rogue for women as any in the world; which did disquiet me, like a fool, and run in my mind a great while.

# [Tuesday 24 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/24/)

Up, and all the morning at [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), and at noon with my clerks to dinner, and then to the office again, busy at the office till six at night, and then by coach to [St. James’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/466/), it being about six at night; my design being to see the ceremonys, this night being the eve of [Christmas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/), at the [Queen’s chapel](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7305/). But it being not begun I to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), and there staid and walked, and then to [the Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1707/), and there drank and talked, and did banter [L&M say “besar”. P.G.] a little [Frank](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10614/), and so to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and sent my coach round, I through [the Park](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/248/) to chapel, where I got in up almost to the rail, and with a great deal of patience staid from nine at night to two in the morning, in a very great crowd; and there expected, but found nothing extraordinary, there being nothing but a high masse. [The Queen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) was there, and some ladies. But, Lord! what an odde thing it was for me to be in a crowd of people, here a footman, there a beggar, here a fine lady, there a zealous poor [papist](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/306/), and here a [Protestant](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7980/), two or three together, come to see the shew. I was afeard of my pocket being picked very much … [But here I did make myself to do la cosa by mere imagination, miranda a jolie mosa and with my yes open, which I never did before — and God forgive me for it, it being in the chapel. – L&M] Their musique very good indeed, but their service I confess too frivolous, that there can be no zeal go along with it, and I do find by them themselves that they do run over their beads with one hand, and point and play and talk and make signs with the other in the midst of their masse. But all things very rich and beautiful; and I see the papists have the wit, most of them, to bring cushions to kneel on, which I wanted, and was mightily troubled to kneel. All being done, and I sorry for my coming, missing of what I expected; which was, to have had a child born and dressed there, and a great deal of do: but we broke up, and nothing like it done: and there I left people receiving the Sacrament: and the Queen gone, and ladies; only my [Lady Castlemayne](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1062/), who looked prettily in her night-clothes, and so took my coach, which waited, and away through [Covent Garden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/126/), to set down two gentlemen and a lady, who come thither to see also, and did make mighty mirth in their talk of the folly of this religion. And so I stopped, having set them down and drank some burnt [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/) at the [Rose Tavern](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11956/) door, while the [constables](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14184/) come, and two or three Bellmen went by… [Continued [tomorrow](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/25/). P.G.]

# [Wednesday 25 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/25/)

[Continued from [yesterday](http://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/24/). P.G.] …it being a fine, light, moonshine morning, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) round [the city](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/), and stopped and dropped money at five or six places, which I was the willinger to do, it being [Christmas-day](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/), and so home, and there find [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) in bed, and [Jane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/149/) and the maids making pyes, and so I to bed, and slept well, and rose about nine, and to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), and there heard a dull sermon of [Mr. Mills](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1215/), but a great many fine people at church; and so home. Wife and [girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) and I alone at dinner — a good Christmas dinner, and all the afternoon at home, my wife reading to me [“The History of the Drummer of Mr. Mompesson,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11957/) which is a strange story of spies, and worth reading indeed. # [Thursday 26 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/26/)

Up and to Westminster, and there to [the Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1050/), and by chance met [Mr. Spicer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1078/) and another [’Chequer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/290/) clerk, and there made them drink, and there talked of the credit the ’Chequer is now come to and will in a little time, and so away homeward, and called at [my bookseller’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11465/), and there bought [Mr. Harrington’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7047/) works, [“Oceana,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11562/)&c., and two other books, which cost me 4 _l._, and so [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there eat a bit, and then with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) to the [King’s playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), and there saw [“The Surprizall;”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11025/) which did not please me to-day, the actors not pleasing me; and especially [Nell’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5037/) acting of a serious part, which she spoils. Here met with [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/), and sat by him, and home by coach with him, and there to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) a while, and then home to supper and to bed. I hear this day that [Mrs. Stewart](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5036/) do at this day keep a great court at [Somerset House](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/243/), with her husband the [Duke of Richmond](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6590/), she being visited for her beauty’s sake by people, as [the Queen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) is, at nights; and they say also that she is likely to go to Court again, and there put my [Lady Castlemayne’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1062/) nose out of joynt. God knows that would make a great turn. This day I was invited to have gone to my cozen [Mary Pepys’](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2934/) burial, my uncle [Thomas’](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2542/) daughter, but could not.

# [Friday 27 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/27/)

Up, and by water to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there walked with [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/) in the [Matted gallery](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5840/) till by and by a [Committee for Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/) met: the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) there; and there I did discourse over to them their condition as to money, which they were all mightily, as I could desire, satisfied with, but the [Duke of Albemarle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/111/), who takes the part of the Guards against us in our supplies of money, which is an odd consideration for a dull, heavy blockhead as he is, understanding no more of either than a goose: but the ability and integrity of [Sir W. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/), in all [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) concernments, I do and must admire. After the Committee up, I and Sir W. Coventry walked an hour in the gallery, talking over many businesses, and he tells me that there are so many things concur to make him and his Fellow Commissioners unable to go through the King’s work that he do despair of it, every body becoming an enemy to them in their retrenchments, and the King unstable, the debts great and the King’s present occasions for money great and many and pressing, the bankers broke and every body keeping in their money, while the times are doubtful what will stand. But he says had they come in two years ago they doubt not to have done what the King would by this time, or were the King in the condition as heretofore, when [the Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/) was great, to be able to have what sums of money they pleased of the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/), and then the ill administration was such that instead of making good use of this power and money he suffered all to go to ruin. But one such sum now would put all upon their legs, and now the King would have the Parliament give him money when they are in an ill humour and will not be willing to give any, nor are very able, and besides every body distrusts what they give the King will be lost; whereas six months hence, when they see that the King can live without them, and is become steady, and to manage what he has well, he doubts not but their doubts would be removed, and would be much more free as well as more able to give him money. He told me how some of his enemies at the Duke of York’s had got the Duke of York’s commission for the Commissioners of his estate changed, and he and [Brouncker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4135/) and [Povy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5263/) left out: that this they did do to disgrace and impose upon him at this time; but that he, though he values not the thing, did go and tell the Duke of York what he heard, and that he did not think that he had given him any reason to do this, out of his belief that he would not be as faithful and serviceable to him as the best of those that have got him put out. Whereupon the Duke of York did say that it arose only from his not knowing whether now he would have time to regard his affairs; and that, if he should, he would put him into the commission with his own hand, though the commission be passed. He answered that he had been faithful to him, and done him good service therein, so long as he could attend it; and if he had been able to have attended it more, he would not have enriched himself with such and such estates as my Lord Chancellor hath got, that did properly belong to his Royal Highness, as being forfeited to the King, and so by the King’s gift given to the Duke of York. Hereupon the Duke of York did call for the commission, and hath since put him in. This he tells me he did only to show his enemies that he is not so low as to be trod on by them, or the Duke hath any so bad opinion of him as they would think.

Here we parted, and I with [Sir H. Cholmly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5179/) went and took a turn into [the Park](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/248/), and there talked of several things, and about [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) particularly, and of his management of his business, and among other discourse about the method he will leave his accounts in if he should suddenly die, he says there is nothing but what is easily understood, but only a sum of 500 _l._ which he has entered given to E. E. S., which in great confidence he do discover to me to be my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/), at the beginning of their contract for the [Mole](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5384/), and I suppose the rest did the like, which was 1500 _l._, which would appear a very odd thing for my Lord to be a profiter by the getting of the contract made for them. But here it puts me into thoughts how I shall own my receiving of 200 _l._ a year from him, but it is his gift, I never asked of him, and which he did to Mr. Povy, and so there is no great matter in it. Thence to other talk. He tells me that the business of getting the [Duchess of Richmond](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5036/) to Court is broke off, [the Duke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6590/) not suffering it; and thereby great trouble is brought among the people that endeavoured it, and thought they had compassed it. And, Lord! to think that at this time the King should mind no other cares but these! He tells me that my [Lord of Canterbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2519/) is a mighty stout man, and a man of a brave, high spirit, and cares not for this disfavour that he is under at Court, knowing that the King cannot take away his profits during his life, and therefore do not value it.1

Thence I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) and wrote a letter to the Duke of York from myself about my clerks extraordinary, which I have employed this war, to prevent my being obliged to answer for what others do without any reason demand allowance for, and so by this means I will be accountable for none but my own, and they shall not have them but upon the same terms that I have, which is a profession that with these helps they will answer to their having performed their duties of their places. So to dinner, and then away by coach to the [Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/131/), and then for speed by water thence to White Hall, and there to our usual attending the Duke of York, and did attend him, where among other things I did present and lodge my letter, and did speed in it as I could wish. Thence home with [Sir W. Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) and [Comm. Middleton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7120/) by coach, and there home and to [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/) with my [wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), [W. Hewer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/), [Mercer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7761/), and [the girle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/), and mighty pleasant all the evening, and so to bed with my wife, which I have not done since her being ill for three weeks or thereabouts.

1.   This character of Archbishop Sheldon does not tally with the scandal that Pepys previously reported of him. Burnet has some passages of importance on this in his “Own Time,” Book II. He affirms that Charles’s final decision to throw over Clarendon was caused by the Chancellor’s favouring Mrs. Stewart’s marriage with the Duke of Richmond. The king had a conference with Sheldon on the removal of Clarendon, but could not convert the archbishop to his view. Lauderdale told Burnet that he had an account of the interview from the king. “The king and Sheldon had gone into such expostulations upon it that from that day forward Sheldon could never recover the king’s confidence.” ↩

# [Saturday 28 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/28/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where busy all the morning, at noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there to dinner with my clerks and [Mr. Pelling](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11258/), and had a very good dinner, among others a haunch of [venison](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/383/) boiled, and merry we were, and I rose soon from dinner, and with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and [girle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) to the [King’s house](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), and there saw [“The Mad Couple,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11618/) which is but an ordinary play; but only [Nell’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5037/) and [Hart’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11087/) mad parts are most excellently done, but especially hers: which makes it a miracle to me to think how ill she do any serious part, as, the other day, just like a fool or changeling; and, in a mad part, do beyond all imitation almost. [It pleased us mightily to see the natural affection of a poor woman, the mother of one of the children brought on the stage: the child crying, she by force got upon the stage, and took up her child and carried it away off of the stage from Hart.]

Many fine faces here to-day. Thence home, and there to the office late, and then home to supper and to bed.

I am told to-day, which troubles me, that great complaint is made upon [the ’Change](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/), among our merchants, that the very [Ostend](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7827/) little pickaroon men-of-war do offer violence to our merchant-men, and search them, beat our masters, and plunder them, upon pretence of carrying Frenchmen’s goods. Lord! what a condition are we come to, and that so soon after a war!

# [Sunday 29 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/29/)

(Lord’s day). Up, and at my chamber all the day, both morning and afternoon (only a little at dinner with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) alone), upon the settling of my [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) accounts towards the evening of all reckonings now against the new year, and here I do see the great folly of letting things go long unevened, it being very hard for me and dangerous to state after things are gone out of memory, and much more would be so should I have died in this time and my accounts come to other hands, to understand which would never be. At night comes [Mrs. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3028/) to see us; and there, among other talk, she tells me that [Mr. William Pen](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2514/), who is lately come over from Ireland, is a [Quaker](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/305/) again, or some very melancholy thing; that he cares for no company, nor comes into any which is a pleasant thing, after his being abroad so long, and [his father](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) such a hypocritical rogue, and at this time an [Atheist](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/368/). She gone, I to my very great content do find my accounts to come very even and naturally, and so to supper and to bed.

# [Monday 30 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/30/)

Up before day, and by coach to Westminster, and there first to [Sir H. Cholmly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5179/), and there I did to my great content deliver him up his little several papers for sums of money paid him, and took his regular receipts upon his orders, wherein I am safe. Thence to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there to visit [Sir G. Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1018/), and there was with him a great while, and [my Lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4039/) and they seem in very good humour, but by and by Sir G. Carteret and I alone, and there we did talk of the ruinous condition we are in, [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) being going to put out of the Council so many able men; such as my [Lord Anglesey](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/887/), [Ashly](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/215/), [Hollis](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/886/), [Secretary Morrice](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5947/) (to bring in [Mr. Trevor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11972/)), and the [Archbishop of Canterbury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2519/), and my [Lord Bridgewater](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11086/). He tells me that this is true, only the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) do endeavour to hinder it, and the Duke of York himself did tell him so: that the King and the Duke of York do not in company disagree, but are friendly; but that there is a core in their hearts, he doubts, which is not to be easily removed; for these men do suffer only for their constancy to the [Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/), or at least from the King’s ill-will against him: that they do now all they can to vilify the clergy, and do accuse [Rochester](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10263/) [Dolben] … [of his being given to boys and of his putting his hand into a gentleman (who now comes to bear evidence against him) his codpiece while they were at table together. – L&M] And so do raise scandals, all that is possible, against other of the Bishops. He do suggest that something is intended for the [Duke of Monmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5315/), and it may be, against [the Queene](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2381/) also: that we are in no manner sure against an invasion the next year: that the [Duke of Buckingham](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2558/) do rule all now, and the Duke of York comes indeed to [the Caball](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13278/), but signifies little there. That this new faction do not endure, nor the King, [Sir W. Coventry](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/830/); but yet that he is so usefull that they cannot be without him; but that he is not now called to the Caball. That my Lord of Buckingham, [Bristoll](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2845/), and [Arlington](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5520/), do seem to agree in these things; but that they do not in their hearts trust one another, but do drive several ways, all of them. In short, he do bless himself that he is no more concerned in matters now; and the hopes he hath of being at liberty, when his accounts are over, to retire into the country. That he do give over the kingdom for wholly lost. So after some other little discourse, I away, meeting with [Mr. Cooling](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1027/). I with him by coach to [the Wardrobe](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/946/), where I never was since [the fire](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10319/) in [Hatton Garden](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10948/), but did not ’light: and he tells me he fears that my [Lord Sandwich](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/112/) will suffer much by [Mr. Townsend’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/947/) being untrue to him, he being now unable to give the [Commissioners of the Treasury](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11226/) an account of his money received by many thousands of pounds, which I am troubled for.

Thence to the [Old Exchange](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/189/) together, he telling me that he believes there will be no such turning out of great men as is talked of, but that it is only to fright people, but I do fear there may be such a thing doing. He do mightily inveigh against the folly of the King to bring his matters to wrack thus, and that we must all be undone without help. I met with Cooling at the [Temple-gate](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/503/), after I had been at both [my](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11024/)[booksellers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11465/) and there laid out several pounds in books now against the new year. From the ’Change (where I met with [Captain Cocke](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3164/), who would have borrowed money of me, but I had the grace to deny him, he would have had 3 or 400 _l._) I with Cocke and [Mr. Temple](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9022/) (whose wife was just now brought to bed of a boy, but he seems not to be at all taken with it, which is a strange consideration how others do rejoice to have a child born), to Sir G. Carteret’s, in [Lincoln’s Inn Fields](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/125/), and there did dine together, there being there, among other company, [Mr. Attorney Montagu](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/563/), and [his fine lady](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3690/), a fine woman. After dinner, I did understand from my [Lady Jemimah](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/114/) that her brother [Hinchingbroke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/113/) business was to be ended this day, as she thinks, towards his match, and they do talk here of their intent to buy themselves some new clothes against the wedding, which I am very glad of. After dinner I did even with Sir G. Carteret the accounts of the interest of the money which I did so long put out for him in [Sir R. Viner’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8584/) hands, and by it I think I shall be a gainer about 28 _l._, which is a very good reward for the little trouble I have had in it. Thence with [Sir Philip Carteret](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8250/) to the [King’s playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), there to see [“Love’s Cruelty,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11973/) an old play, but which I have not seen before; and in the first act [Orange Moll](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10310/) come to me, with one of our porters by my house, to tell me that [Mrs. Pierce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/785/) and [Knepp](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9483/) did dine at my house to-day, and that I was desired to come [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/). So I went out presently, and by coach home, and they were just gone away so, after a very little stay with [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), I took coach again, and to the King’s playhouse again, and come in the fourth act; and it proves to me a very silly play, and to everybody else, as far as I could judge. But the jest is, that here telling Moll how I had lost my journey, she told me that Mrs. Knepp was in the house, and so shews me to her, and I went to her, and sat out the play, and then with her to [Mrs. Manuel’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11497/), where Mrs. Pierce was, and her [boy](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9472/) and [girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9044/); and here I did hear Mrs. Manuel and one of the Italians, her gallant, sing well. But yet I confess I am not delighted so much with it, as to admire it: for, not understanding the words, I lose the benefit of the vocalitys of the musick, and it proves only instrumental; and therefore was more pleased to hear Knepp sing two or three little English things that I understood, though the composition of the other, and performance, was very fine. Thence, after sitting and talking a pretty while, I took leave and left them there, and so to my bookseller’s, and paid for the books I had bought, and away home, where I told my wife where I had been. But she was as mad as a devil, and nothing but ill words between us all the evening while we sat at [cards](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/797/) — [W. Hewer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1082/) and [the girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) by — even to gross ill words, which I was troubled for, but do see that I must use policy to keep her spirit down, and to give her no offence by my being with Knepp and Pierce, of which, though she will not own it, yet she is heartily jealous. At last it ended in few words and my silence (which for fear of growing higher between us I did forbear), and so to supper and to bed without one word one to another.

This day I did carry money out, and paid several debts. Among others, [my tailor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9587/), and shoemaker, and draper, [Sir W. Turner](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3725/), who begun to talk of the [Commission of accounts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/12029/), wherein he is one; but though they are the greatest people that ever were in the nation as to power, and like to be our judges, yet I did never speak one word to him of desiring favour, or bidding him joy in it, but did answer him to what he said, and do resolve to stand or fall by my silent preparing to answer whatever can be laid to me, and that will be my best proceeding, I think. This day I got a little rent in my new fine [camlett](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11928/) cloak with the latch of Sir G. Carteret’s door; but it is darned up at my tailor’s, that it will be no great blemish to it; but it troubled me. I could not but observe that Sir Philip Carteret would fain have given me my going into a play; but yet, when he come to the door, he had no money to pay for himself, I having refused to accept of it for myself, but was fain; and I perceive he is known there, and do run upon the score for plays, which is a shame; but I perceive always he is in want of money.1

In the pit I met with [Sir Ch. North](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/725/), formerly Mr. North, who was with my Lord at sea; and he, of his own accord, was so silly as to tell me he [is married](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11974/); and for her quality (being a Lord’s daughter, my Lord Grey), and person, and beauty, and years, and estate, and disposition, he is the happiest man in the world. I am sure he is an ugly fellow; but a good scholar and sober gentleman; and heir to his father, now [Lord North](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/726/), the [old Lord](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14142/) being dead.

1.   The practice of gallants attending the theatre without payment is illustrated by Mr. Lowe in his “Betterton,” from Shadwell’s “True Widow”:

# [Tuesday 31 December 1667](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1667/12/31/)

Up, without words to [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/), or few, and those not angry, and so to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), and there waited a long time, while the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) was with [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) in [the Caball](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/13278/), and there I and [Creed](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/507/) stayed talking without, in the [Vane-Room](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7036/), and I perceive all people’s expectation is, what will be the issue of this great business of putting these great Lords out of the council and power, the quarrel, I perceive, being only their standing against the will of the King in the business of [the Chancellor](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/804/). Anon the Duke of York comes out, and then to a [committee of Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5243/), where my [Lord Middleton](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7228/) did come to-day, and seems to me but a dull, heavy man; but he is a great soldier, and stout, and a needy Lord, which will still keep that poor garrison from ever coming to be worth anything to the King. Here, after a short meeting, we broke up, and I home to the office, where they are sitting, and so I to them, and having done our business rose, and I [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner with my people, and there dined with me my uncle [Thomas](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2542/), with a mourning hat-band on, for his daughter [Mary](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2934/), and here I and my people did discourse of the [Act for the accounts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/12029/), which do give the greatest power to these people, as they report that have read it (I having not yet read it, and indeed its nature is such as I have no mind to go about to read it, for fear of meeting matter in it to trouble me), that ever was given to any subjects, and too much also. After dinner with my wife and [girl](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11640/) to [Unthanke’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1201/), and there left her, and I to Westminster, and there to [Mrs. Martin’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1157/), and did hazer con elle what I desired, and there did drink with her, and find fault with [her husband’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7729/) wearing of too fine clothes, by which I perceive he will be a beggar, and so after a little talking I away and took up my wife again, and so home and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where [Captain Perryman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10970/) did give me an account, walking in the garden, how the seamen of England are discouraged by want of money (or otherwise by being, as he says, but I think without cause, by their being underrated) so far as that he thinks the greatest part are gone abroad or going, and says that it is known that there are Irish in the town, up and down, that do labour to entice the seamen out of the nation by giving them 3 _l._ in hand, and promise of 40 _s._ per month, to go into the [King of France’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5855/) service, which is a mighty shame, but yet I believe is true. I did advise with him about my little vessel, [“The Maybolt,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/11665/) which he says will be best for me to sell, though my employing her to [Newcastle](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7005/) this winter, and the next spring, for coles, will be a gainful trade, but yet make me great trouble, but I will think of it, and so to my office, ended my letters, and so home to supper and to bed, good friends with my wife.

Thus ends the year, with great happiness to myself and family as to health and good condition in the world, blessed be God for it! only with great trouble to my mind in reference to the publick, there being little hopes left but that the whole nation must in a very little time be lost, either by troubles at home, the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) being dissatisfied, and the King led into unsettled councils by some about him, himself considering little, and divisions growing between the King and Duke of York; or else by foreign invasion, to which we must submit if any, at this bad point of time, should come upon us, which the King of France is well able to do. These thoughts, and some cares upon me, concerning my standing in this Office when the Committee of Parliament shall come to examine our Navy matters, which they will now shortly do. I pray God they may do the kingdom service therein, as they will have sufficient opportunity of doing it!

# Diary entries from December 1666

# [Saturday 1 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/01/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning. At [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, and then abroad walking to the [Old Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4002/), and in my way I did see a cellar in [Tower Streete](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1117/) in a very fresh fire, the late great winds having blown it up.1 It seemed to be only of log-wood, that Hath kept [the fire](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10319/) all this while in it. Going further, I met my late [Lord Mayor Bludworth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5187/), under whom [the City](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/) was burned, and went with him by water to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/). But, Lord! the silly talk that this fellow had, only how ready he would be to part with all his estate in these difficult times to advance [the King’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) service, and complaining that now, as every body did lately in the fire, every body endeavours to save himself, and let the whole perish: but a very weak man he seems to be. I left him at White Hall, he giving 6 _d._ towards the boat, and I to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), where I was again defeated in my expectation of [Burroughs](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8607/). However, I was not much sorry for it, but by coach [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), in the evening, calling at [Faythorne’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/907/), buying three of my [Lady Castlemayne’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1062/) heads, printed this day, which indeed is, as to the head, I think, a very fine picture, and like her. I did this afternoon get [Mrs. Michell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1101/) to let me only have a sight of a pamphlet lately printed, but suppressed and much called after, called [“The Catholique’s Apology;”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10595/) lamenting the severity of the [Parliament](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/334/) against them, and comparing it with the lenity of other princes to [Protestants](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7980/); giving old and late instances of their loyalty to their princes, whatever is objected against them; and excusing their disquiets in [Queen Elizabeth’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5307/) time, for that it was impossible for them to think her a lawfull Queen, if [Queen Mary](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10596/), who had been owned as such, were so; one being the daughter of the true, and the other of a false wife: and that of the [Gunpowder Treason](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/313/), by saying that it was only the practice of some of us, if not the King, to trepan some of their religion into it, it never being defended by the generality of their Church, nor indeed known by them; and ends with a large Catalogue, in red letters, of the [Catholiques](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/306/) which have lost their lives in the quarrel of the [late King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/624/) and this. The thing is very well writ indeed. So home to my letters, and then to my supper and to bed.

1.   The fire continued burning in some cellars of the ruins of the city for four months, though it rained in the month of October ten days without ceasing (Rugge’s “Diurnal”). — B. ↩

# [Sunday 2 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/02/)

(Lord’s day). Up, and to [church](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1214/), and after church [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, where I met [Betty Michell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5329/) and her [husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9771/), very merry at dinner, and after dinner, having borrowed [Sir W. Pen’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/619/) coach, we to Westminster, they two and [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) and I to [Mr. Martin’s](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7729/), where find the company almost all come to the christening of [Mrs. Martin’s](https://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1157/)[child](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10567/), a girl. A great deal of good plain company. After sitting long, till the church was done, the Parson comes, and then we to christen the child. I was Godfather, and [Mrs. Holder](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6677/) ([her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2187/), a good man, I know well), and a pretty lady, that waits, it seems, on my [Lady Bath](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/14063/), at [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), her name, [Mrs. Noble](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10598/), were Godmothers. After the christening comes in the [wine](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/309/) and the [sweetmeats](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4140/), and then to prate and tattle, and then very good company they were, and I among them. Here was old [Mrs. Michell](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1101/) and [Howlett](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3065/), and several married women of [the Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/), whom I knew mayds. Here was also [Mrs. Burroughs](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8607/) and [Mrs. Bales](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/7603/), the young widow, whom I led home, and having staid till the moon was up, I took my pretty gossip to White Hall with us, and I saw her in her lodging, and then my owne company again took coach, and no sooner in the coach but something broke, that we were fain there to stay till a smith could be fetched, which was above an hour, and then it costing me 6 _s._ to mend. Away round by the wall and [Cow Lane](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10599/), for fear it should break again; and in pain about the coach all the way. But to ease myself therein Betty Michell did sit at the same end with me … [and there con su mano under my manteau, I did pull off her cheirotheca and did tocar mi cosa con su mano through my chemise, but yet so as to hazer me hazer la grande cosa — and she did let me hazerle sin mucho trabaho. – L&M] Being very much pleased with this, we at last come home, and so to supper, and then sent them by boat home, and we to bed.

When I come home I went to [Sir W. Batten’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/852/), and there I hear more ill newes still: that all our New England fleete, which went out lately, are put back a third time by foul weather, and dispersed, some to one port and some to another; and their convoys also to [Plymouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5849/); and whether any of them be lost or not, we do not know. This, added to all the rest, do lay us flat in our hopes and courages, every body prophesying destruction to the nation.

# [Monday 3 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/03/)

Up, and, among a great many people that come to speak with me, one was my [Lord Peterborough’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3178/) gentleman, who comes to me to dun me to get some money advanced for my Lord; and I demanding what newes, he tells me that at Court they begin to fear the business of Scotland more and more; and that the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/) intends to go to the North to raise an army, and that [the King](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/344/) would have some of the Nobility and others to go and assist; but they were so served the last year, among others his Lord, in raising forces at their own charge, for fear of the French invading us, that they will not be got out now, without money advanced to them by the King, and this is like to be the King’s case for certain, if ever he comes to have need of any army.

He and others gone, I by water to Westminster, and there to the [Exchequer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/242/), and put my [tallys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8499/) in a way of doing for the last quarter. But my not following it the last week has occasioned the clerks some trouble, which I am sorry for, and they are mad at. Thence at noon [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), and there find [Kate Joyce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1105/), who dined with me: [Her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1107/) and she are weary of their new life of being an Innkeeper, and will leave it, and would fain get some office; but I know none the foole is fit for, but would be glad to help them, if I could, though they have enough to live on, God be thanked! though their loss hath been to the value of 3000 _l._[W. Joyce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1090/) now has all the trade, she says, the trade being come to that end of the towne. She dined with me, [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) being ill of her months in bed. I left her with my wife, and away myself to [Westminster Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/128/) by appointment and there found out [Burroughs](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8607/), and I took her by coach as far as the [Lord Treasurer’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/4111/) and called at the cake house by [Hales’s](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2206/), and there in the coach eat and drank and then carried her home … [with much ado making her to tocar mi cosa, she being endeed very averse a alguna cosa of that kind. – L&M] So having set her down in the palace I to the [Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1707/), and there did the first time ‘baiser’ the little [sister](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10614/) of [Sarah](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8177/) that is come into her place, and so away by coach home, where to my [vyall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/461/) and supper and then to bed, being weary of the following of my pleasure and sorry for my omitting (though with a true salvo to my vowes) the stating my last month’s accounts in time, as I should, but resolve to settle, and clear all my business before me this month, that I may begin afresh the next yeare, and enjoy some little pleasure freely at [Christmasse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/314/). So to bed, and with more cheerfulness than I have done a good while, to hear that for certain the Scott rebells are all routed; they having been so bold as to come within three miles of [Edinburgh](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10615/), and there given two or three repulses to the King’s forces, but at last were mastered. Three or four hundred killed or taken, among which their leader, one [Wallis](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10616/), and seven ministers, they having all taken the Covenant a few days before, and sworn to live and die in it, as they did; and so all is likely to be there quiet again. There is also the very good newes come of four New-England ships come home safe to [Falmouth](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10617/) with [masts](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/5619/) for the King; which is a blessing mighty unexpected, and without which, if for nothing else, we must have failed the next year. But God be praised for thus much good fortune, and send us the continuance of his favour in other things! So to bed.

# [Tuesday 4 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/04/)

Up, and to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the morning. At noon dined at [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/). After dinner presently to my office, and there late and then home to even my Journall and accounts, and then to supper much eased in mind, and last night’s good news, which is more and more confirmed with particulars to very good purpose, and so to bed.

# [Wednesday 5 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/05/)

Up, and by water to [White Hall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/180/), where we did much business before the [Duke of York](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/800/), which being done, I away [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) by water again, and there to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) till noon busy. At noon home, and [Goodgroome](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2745/) dined with us, who teaches [my wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) to sing. After dinner I did give him my song, [“Beauty retire,”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9571/) which he has often desired of me, and without flattery I think is a very good song. He gone, I to the office, and there late, very busy doing much business, and then home to supper and talk, and then scold with my wife for not reckoning well the times that her musique master hath been with her, but setting down more than I am sure, and did convince her, they had been with her, and in an ill humour of anger with her to bed.

# [Thursday 6 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/06/)

Up, but very good friends with [her](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) before I rose, and so to [the office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/), where we sat all the forenoon, and then [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/) to dinner, where [Harman](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6860/) dined with us, and great sport to hear him tell how [Will Joyce](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1090/) grows rich by the custom of [the City](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/275/) coming to his end of the towne, and how he rants over [his brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1107/) and [sister](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1105/) for their keeping an Inne, and goes thither and tears like a prince, calling him hosteller and his sister hostess. Then after dinner, my wife and [brother](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/117/), in another habit; go out to see a play; but I am not to take notice that I know of my brother’s going. So I to the office, where very busy till late at night, and then home. My wife not pleased with the play, but thinks that it is because she is grown more critical than she used to be, but my brother she says is mighty taken with it. So to supper and to bed.

This day, in [the Gazette](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/9931/), is the whole story of defeating the Scotch rebells, and of the creation of the [Duke of Cambridge](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/6506/), Knight of the Garter.

# [Friday 7 December 1666](https://www.pepysdiary.com/diary/1666/12/07/)

Up, and by water to [the Exchequer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/242/), where I got my [tallys](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8499/) finished for the last quarter for [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/), and having paid all my fees I to [the Swan](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1707/), whither I sent for some [oysters](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/373/), and thither comes [Mr. Falconbridge](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/3671/) and [Spicer](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1078/) and many more clerks; and there we eat and drank, and a great deal of their sorry discourse, and so parted, and I by coach [home](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1023/), meeting [Balty](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/631/) in the streete about [Charing Crosse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/138/) walking, which I am glad to see and spoke to him about his mustering business, I being now to give an account how the several muster-masters have behaved themselves, and so home to dinner, where finding the cloth laid and much crumpled but clean, I grew angry and flung the [trenchers](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/1779/) about the room, and in a mighty heat I was: so a clean cloth was laid, and my poor [wife](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/150/) very patient, and so to dinner, and in comes [Mrs. Barbara Sheldon](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8955/), now Mrs. Wood, and dined with us, she mighty fine, and lives, I perceive, mighty happily, which I am glad [of] for her sake, but hate [her husband](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10246/) for a block-head in his choice. So away after dinner, leaving my wife and her, and by water to [the Strand](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/245/), and so to [the King’s playhouse](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/475/), where two acts were almost done when I come in; and there I sat with my cloak about my face, and saw the remainder of [“The Mayd’s Tragedy;”](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/10618/) a good play, and well acted, especially by the younger [Marshall](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/8437/), who is become a pretty good actor, and is the first play I have seen in either of the houses since before the great [plague](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/301/), they having acted now about fourteen days publickly. But I was in mighty pain lest I should be seen by any body to be at a play. Soon as done I home, and then to [my office](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/483/) awhile, and then home and spent the night evening my [Tangier](http://www.pepysdiary.com/encyclopedia/2783/) accounts, much to my satisfaction, and then to supper, and mighty good friends with my poor wife, and so to bed.
